title: My niece played my game for over an hour and was thrilled!
author: Emu_Fast
selftext:
Having family over this weekend, I got the chance to show my 11 year old niece what I've been working on. She is a little 'bookish,' is big into the sciences, and is overall super bright.

My game is about creating a world, determining continent shape and ice age severity. Then you simulate a human culture as it grows and expands. It focuses on ancient humans and hominids, starting roughly 80k years BC. Tribemembers sort into duties of hunting, foraging, fishing, or working in camp. You play as a deity with various powers to steer the elements and inspire human innovation.

The mechanics of my game I've been frustrated with, no matter what I try, I can't get the mechanics to work out as I've envisioned them. Particularly, having a turn based hunting mechanics where you stalk herds, and then either position around them for an ambush or simply chase them as persistence hunters. Also, I've got a slightly-ARPG format for sending hunters into caves to clear them of large predators or rival hominids. Yet, most of the mechanics are messy, unfinished, not responsive or strategic in the ways that will make it shine.  
  
As a dad of a preschooler, with a full-time job and an endless remodel, using Claude has been a gamechanger. Designs sitting in my notebook for 15+ years are finally seeing the light of day. Yet, I've felt extraordinarily far away from having something polished enough to sit down and "play."

Yet, my niece was drawn in. The bloodlust as she took down her first antelope was real. Exploring the world and seeing all the different biomes was novel again. Seeing her drawn into the story of making a prehistoric ancestor deity was fantastic. When she finished, she turned to me and said, "how did you do this? This is amazing!"

She learned about neandethals and denisovans, tried to devise her own hunting tactics, learned that dogs were domesticated only \~20k years ago.

All this to say, don't get discouraged, what you built might be a lot more entertaining and fun than you give yourself credit for, even if the mechanics are still being worked out. Keep at it!

comments.author: samcripp
comments.body:
Your game could get a million downloads, and I assure you, nothing will beat the high of watching someone you love or care enjoy your creation.

Good on you buddy!

replies.author: Emu_Fast
replies.body: 100% agree. I'd be happy for 10 downloads to start though 😁

comments.author: asimpleabstraction
comments.body: I think the kids enablement subject is one of the big reasons AI game dev will find it's niche. It's always been so hard to get kids to build games because of how high the barrier to entry is.

replies.author: samcripp
replies.body: love2d is ana amazing tool for getting kids acquainted with programing. AI is great, im not hating, just saying, if you want a kiddo to learn the old school way, love2d is amazing for that.

comments.author: Boring-Telephone-834
comments.body: my nephew got obsessed with a similar game last year, spent hours tweaking climate settings just to see how a desert would spread. the moment he realized he could make a whole ecosystem from scratch? he was hooked. seems like the same magic.

comments.author: Hfcsmakesmefart
comments.body: I’m working on the same mechanics, turn based “hunting”. It took me A WHILE to get the input and I’m still not happy with it, but the surrounding mechanic works IMO, now just need to figure out how to program the AI to do it

comments.author: derLeisemitderLaute
comments.body: I fully agree. Usually I just make games for myself because I have a lot of ideas for projects. Last week I played with my girlfriend my prototype of my new board game and it was so satisfying to see how much fun she had
